speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CHANGE IN HOURS OF SITTING ON FEBRUARY 6
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. members are aware, the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, Sir Anthony Eden, will be arriving in Ottawa tomorrow afternoon. Arrangements have been made to have our distinguished guest address the members of both houses of parliament in this chamber at 2.30 o'clock on Monday afternoon. Because of these arrangements it will be necessary to delay the opening of the ordinary proceedings of the house until 4.30 o'clock on Monday. If I may have the unanimous consent of the house I should like to move:
That when this house adjourns tomorrow it stand adjourned until Monday next at 4.30 o'clock in the afternoon.
I understand that the ordinary tickets for the gallery have been cancelled for that occasion and special tickets have been distributed to the whips to be made available to the members of this house who wish to have guests attend the ceremony. It would be appreciated, of course, if all hon. members could be in their seats a few minutes before 2.30 in the afternoon.
We have all received from you, sir, a very kind invitation to attend in your chambers immediately after the ceremony to have the privilege of meeting with the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, Mr. Selwyn Lloyd.

the second reading of Bill No. 2, to amend the Interest Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the Interest Act, as it now stands, does not provide any limit on the interest that may be charged in this country. In certain fields there are limits on the interest rates that may be charged but those limits are placed there by special acts of parliament. Apart from money lent under the Small Loans Act, the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Bank Act and so on, there is no legal limit to the amount of interest that may be charged. In the fields where there is no limit to the amount of interest that may be charged, large sums of money at very high rates are being made available.
We have already been told that an amendment or amendments to the Small Loans Act will be presented at this session. My understanding is that the bill covering the amendment or amendments will be referred to the banking and commerce committee for study, a move that I welcome. But at this time I want to express the hope that, when the subject matter of that bill is referred to the banking and commerce committee, the members of the committee will be given perfect freedom to inquire into interest rates as they are levied by all companies and business firms in this country. I am hopeful that the discussion that takes place in the banking and commerce committee may be free and that we shall be able to acquire there all the information that may be necessary to write into the Interest Act a definite limit, and one that may be as low as practicable.
When a week ago I moved second reading of Bill No. 3 having to do with limiting the interest that may be charged under the Small Loans Act, a government member moved the adjournment of the debate. The discussion was stopped. At this time I want to express the hope that the government will not have one of its members move the adjournment of this debate but that rather it will allow the debate to go on today just as long as there are any hon. members wishing to take part in it. I do not think the government at any time should use its overwhelming majority in order to cut off discussion.

After listening to the debate that took place on the Small Loans Act one might draw the inference that as long as we have the Small Loans Act in operation loan sharks, in the sense of persons or corporations, are not able to charge excessive rates of interest. The fact is that loan sharks-if you wish to call them that-are free to operate in Canada provided they are not small loan companies making small loans as defined by the Small Loans Act. In other words, as I understand the law, it is perfectly legal for an individual to make a private loan to any other individual at any rate of interest that may be agreed upon. It is perfectly legal for a finance company-an acceptance corporation, as they are often called-to make any charges that may be agreed upon between the purchaser of an article and the company that is financing that purchase.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If he sets out the effective rate of interest in the document.

I understand further that there is no limit to the interest or rate, or whatever name you may wish to call it, that may be charged by a business firm in providing credit for instalment purchases. I am moving this bill in the hope that there may be established in Canada, on all loans that are made on all instalment buying, an interest or rate limitation. I have suggested in this bill

as I suggested in another bill to amend the Small Loans Act-that that rate should not be more than 12 per cent per annum. When I think of the lower rates at which banks are able to lend money and when I think of the experience that credit unions have had from one end of this country to the other in lending money at a maximum rate of 12 per cent and in many instances at the bank rate of interest, I can see no good reason why a limitation should not be fixed on the interest rates that may be charged on all credit that is made available.
The acceptance corporations-that is the finance companies-from what I have been able to ascertain from making inquiries, all charge a rate in excess of 12 per cent. Hence the passage of this bill would place a definite limit on the rates that may be charged by acceptance corporations. As the result of further inquiries I have made with respect to the rates that are charged, it seems to me that a rate of 18 per cent, 20 per cent or 22 per cent is a common one. The effect of this bill would therefore be to reduce substantially the charges that may be made by those companies. Hence, in my opinion, the result would be a substantial saving to the people of this country.
The amount of money that is made available by acceptance corporations is tremendous.

The amount of money that is made available for instalment purchases of all kinds is large and growing. As a matter of fact, it now appears that the total amount of retail instalment sales in 1955 in Canada is likely to exceed the sum of $1 billion. Retail instalment sales include the purchase of such things as passenger cars, radio and television sets, electric and gas household appliances, furniture and other consumers' goods including clothing and jewelery.
The large item in this list is the item for the purchase of automobiles. Instalment credit for the purchase of new passenger cars in 1953 amounted to $252 million. Instalment credit for the purchase of used passenger cars in that year amounted to $321 million. Most of those purchases are made under what is known as a conditional sales contract. As I understand it, the purchaser has no equity in the automobile that he is purchasing, for example, until the last payment is made; and if he should fail to make a payment at any time, the automobile can be repossessed without much trouble. Since it is a conditional sales contract the purchaser is not entitled to any equity in the automobile even though he may have paid a large part of the purchase price.
On speaking to automobile dealers and implement dealers in various parts of this country, I have been informed by them that not only is there a conditional sales contract as far as the purchaser is concerned but that the same type of thing is worked by the acceptance corporation on the degler himself, and that if there is any loss whatsoever because of the conditional sales contract, the dealer himself will be held responsible for the unpaid balances. Dealers have said to me that, two or three years ago, when things were booming on the prairies-and I am thinking of the prairies particularly-they considered that their net worth was $100,000, $200,000 or $300,000; but because of the conditional sales contract as it has been applied to dealers, and because of the rapid drop in purchasing, they felt that their total net worth -in certain instances approaching a quarter of a million dollars-was in fact at stake. These dealers, because of this type of contract and because of the high rates that are charged, felt that they might lose the total equity they had in their business. In addition to that, the customer would be losing the equity he might have had in the machine he purchased.
This business is very large and very profitable. I have the profit statistics in my hands for four acceptance corporations. The first one is the Union Acceptance Company. In
Interest Act
1948 that company made a profit of $22,500. Six years later, in 1954, it made a profit of over $302,000, an increase in profit of 1,239 per cent. The Laurentide corporation, another acceptance corporation, made a profit of over $30,000 in 1946, and this has been increased to $320,000 in 1954, an increase of 954 per cent within that period. The Industrial Acceptance made a profit of $53,000 in 1946, and 8 years later made a profit of $6,837,000, an increase of 2,596 per cent within that period. The Traders Finance Corporation in 1946 made a profit of $483,000, and in 1954 made a profit of $4,401,000, an increase in the 8-year period of 810 per cent. Clearly, the business of providing money by the acceptance corporations for the purpose of automobiles and other consumer goods is a very lucrative one. It is one which I believe should be inquired into by the banking and commerce committee. Possibly if we had a thorough inquiry into the business practices of the acceptance corporations, into the rates they are charging and into the profits they are making, there could in fact be a decided reduction in the charges they make with a very beneficial result to Canadian consumers.
That is one large field but there is another large field of consumer credit and that is the field of instalment purchases through retail companies. In this field I find that the interest rates or charges, whatever you may wish to term them, go up even higher than the rates charged by the acceptance company. The hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Ellis) a few days ago put on the record in detail the charges made by Eaton's and Simpsons-Sears on the smallest purchase that could be made under the instalment plan. He pointed out that the effective rate on a small purchase was 54 per cent. It is true that as the amount of the purchase increases the rate goes down, but in all instances the rates are considerably higher than the bank rates. In most instances they are from 15 per cent to 35 per cent.
I have quite a number of examples of charges made on the instalment plan, and I shall refer to one at this time. There was an interest charge of 6-25 made on an unpaid balance of $60, repayable in $6 monthly payments. On that unpaid balance of $60, Eaton's or Simpsons-Sears charged an effective rate of 23 per cent. I should like the banking and commerce committee to have before it witnesses from big corporations such- as Simpsons-Sears and Eaton's which do such a tremendous business from one end of this nation to the other. I should like to ascertain from them, if we could, the amount of profit that they acquire because of their credit business and see to what extent the total profits of these huge companies are derived, not from

Interest Act
the amount of profit they make from the actual sale but from the profit they make through the extension of credit.
I have visited a great many homes, as most members of parliament do. I know it is a common practice, it is almost a general practice, for the housewife to have credit accounts with the big mail order houses. I have made purchases at such firms as Simpsons-Sears, and instead of telling me the article was $5.00, for example, the clerk would say to me, "What is your account number?" I said, "I have not got an account number." I felt rather guilty that I did not have an account number because the attitude they seemed to take was that if you did not have an account number you were a bit of an oddity, a bit of a piker. I said, "No, I do not come to Regina very often so I think I will pay cash." It is very simple to get credit. The charges that are made are very high. I imagine a great many purchasers not only do not understand the rate of charge, but in fact have a difficult time meeting their monthly payments because of the very high rate charged.
I am hopeful that witnesses from these two large companies, from some of these acceptance corporations and small loan companies may be brought before a committee of this house and questioned. If members of parliament had such witnesses before them, they could go into the profits that are made by these corporations and then if desirable introduce legislation to reduce the rate that might be charged. As a consequence, I am certain we would save the consumers, the ordinary rank and file of the Canadian people, ten of millions of dollars within a one-year period. We would not have to reduce the rate too much to save many millions of dollars when one bears in mind that, according to the Bank of Canada statistical summary, $2 billion is being lent in credit of one kind or another. Of course, that is not only credit that is being made available and on which very high interest rates may be charged.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask how much of that $2 billion is bank loans?

I have not got the statistics at this time. There would be a considerable portion of it in bank loans. I do, however, have the amount of retail instalment purchasers to which I referred a moment ago. [ made the statement that on the basis of the information available today it might be that retail instalment credit in 1955 would exceed a billion dollars. If you want to confine yourself to the billion dollar figure only and to say nothing about the high interest rate that may be charged by individuals, the high interest rates that may be charged on

second mortgages, I think it is fair to say that many millions of dollars would be saved by the Canadian people if a move were made to reduce interest rates.
One hon. member of the house spoke to me yesterday about a practice that was being followed by people in the business of constructing homes.
It was pointed out to me that the amount of money made available under the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is not sufficient to pay the total cost of construction, and that very often the purchaser of the house does not have the total cash payment required. Therefore, the contractor takes a second mortgage on the house, and that second mortgage is then taken to a finance company which purchases it at a substantial discount. It is true that if a limitation were put on the amount that may be charged for second mortgages, the amount of money available for such second mortgages in all probability would be reduced, and unless something else were done the single act of reducing the interest rate that may be charged on second mortgages would perhaps make it more difficult for individuals to purchase houses.
At this point I should like to read a statement taken from an article in the Chatelaine magazine of January, 1956. It reads as follows:
Avoid second mortgages like the plague. Rates go as high as 10 per cent, with discounts of 15 to 25 per cent. This means that if you take out a $5,000 second mortgage, the lender may only give you $4,000 cash (keeping a discount of $1,000) but you will have to pay the high interest rate on the full amount of $5,000. Thus the discount is a way for the lender to get a much higher true rate of interest on his loan than the stated rate.
The fact that houses are being made available, with second mortgages carrying an effective high interest rate, I believe to some extent at any rate undermines the purpose of the National Housing Act. The purpose of that act was to make houses available to purchasers at a reasonable rate of interest. Therefore, in the whole field of credit the government should take certain very definite additional steps. Besides placing a limit on the interest rate, the government should consider, as, passing a new act of parliament that might be called a family welfare loans act, an act which would provide a small percentage guarantee to the chartered banks to encourage them to make loans to families for ordinary consumer credit purchases, the type of purchases for which they are now paying very high rates.
As a result of the experience of the government with the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the National Housing Act and other acts

of parliament, an act such as I have suggested would be effective in making money available to Canadians at a low rate of interest and would substitute for any money sources that might be dried up as a result of limiting interest rates to 12 per cent.
I should like to see similar guarantees given under such an act, and under all other acts of this nature, to credit unions. Credit unions in Canada are an important source of credit. They are growing in importance. Over the years they have proved their soundness. I believe the government would be wise to encourage the use of credit union facilities by extending to credit unions in every instance the same type of guarantee that is now extended to the chartered banks, so that in the field of making money available to ordinary consumers the credit unions of this nation would be placed on an equal footing with the chartered banks. If that were done the credit unions would be able to function with a loss ratio not any larger, and very likely even smaller, than the very small and commendable loss ratio now experienced by the chartered banks in this lending field.
As has already been said in this house by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight), another thing the government should do is to require all firms, all corporations, all small-loan companies and persons in the field of lending money, to state the effective rate of interest per annum. When a customer comes in and asks for something on the instalment plan he should be immediately informed before the transaction takes place that if he obtains credit of this nature the interest rate will be 10 per cent, 20 per cent, 30 per cent, or whatever the figure may be. If that were done, it would make it much more difficult for those loan companies and corporations to charge an exorbitant rate of interest.
The first action the government should take is to place a definite ceiling on the interest charges that may be made, not only by small-loan companies, but also by acceptance corporations, by large retail firms and by individuals whenever credit is made available.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. member for Assiniboia that this bill should be referred to the banking and commerce committee in order that there may be a thorough investigation into the subject of credit buying. Most of us are familiar with a number of the practices to which he has referred, practices that may be described as very undesirable ones and I think justifiably referred to in many instances as a racket. However, I must admit that
Interest Act
when I first read this bill I was not too well impressed by it. It seems to me that a rate of interest of 12 per cent in an act of this kind is too high. It is true it is only a ceiling; it is true there is no ceiling at the present time; but it does seem to me that when you put a ceiling of 12 per cent into an act you are actually implying that a rate of interest of 12 per cent may be justified under certain circumstances. With one or two minor exceptions I do not think that is the case, and those exceptions can be taken care of by federal legislation.
It seems to me in the past there have been a number of cases where 12 per cent has been charged; for instance, to farmers. As a farmer I have paid 12 per cent. In the early days it was a very common practice to charge a rate of 8 per cent on loans for hail insurance. But the minute that loan became overdue the rate rose to 12 per cent. I have paid that. The due date was October 1,' a date, of course, that no farmer could meet. On farm machinery the rate was 7 per cent until due, and then it became 10 per cent to 12 per cent. We all know that in the vast majority of cases it was not possible for a farmer to pay the note when it became due, therefore in a very short time he was paying 10 per cent and 12 per cent. I am glad to say that practice has ceased to a very large extent, but there are still instances where those rates prevail.
It seems to me the only instance where 12 per cent might be justified would be in regard to small loans, but small loans are covered by a federal statute and therefore would not come under this act. Small-loan companies operating outside a federal charter no doubt would feel they could not carry on their business at a rate of 8 per cent. If we put a ceiling of 8 per cent in the act, then I presume they would immediately apply for a federal charter in order to get the protection of the act. I do not like the idea of putting a ceiling of 12 per cent into an act of this kind because, as I say, it does imply, or appears to imply, that a rate of 12 per cent could be justified under certain circumstances.
I would far rather see the rate of interest set at 7 per cent or 8 per cent, and then let us pass federal legislation to take care of cases where a larger rate may not have been fair. But, in the meantime, in view of the fact that this legislation would prevent a higher rate being charged, I would support the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I am told that in the early days of Christianity it was considered to be against the teachings of the church to charge any

Interest Act
rate of interest at all, and those members of the Christian community who were found guilty of having lent money at a rate of interest were excommunicated. I think we have come a long, long way from that early concept which was held by people toward the use of money. I fail to see how we can set maximum rates of interest that some money lenders in Canada are permitted to charge and then claim to be logical when we say that all others not covered are outside the law in so far as they may charge whatever rate of interest they are able to get.
The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) placed on the record the other day some statistics concerning the operations of the personal loan department of the Canadian Bank of Commerce. Those statistics revealed that although the Bank of Commerce through its personal loan department charges less than 11 per cent interest they still show a net profit of -77 per cent. I think most of us are aware that over a period of many years the Bank of Montreal has made personal loans available to its customers at the rate of 6 per cent per annum on the minimum monthly balance. I am quite willing to concede that possibly the Bank of Montreal is doing this in the interests of good public relations and that it has to rely on its earnings on larger loans in order to break even.
I am very pleased to note the rapid growth throughout Canada of thousands of credit unions none of which charges more than 12 per cent per annum. A larger number of them find at the end of each year that they are able to supply their customers or members with a rebate of some of the interest that has been paid. We can readily see that the business of lending money is growing rapidly in Canada and the number of individuals, organizations and institutions that are engaging in this practice is steadily increasing. When we look at some of the statistics available to us it is small wonder that the number is growing. It is apparently a very easy way to make a living.
I must say to my shame that I recently visited a cousin of mine who had sold his legitimate businesses. I asked him what he was planning to do now and he replied that he intended to lend out his money because for every $10,000 he had he could arrange to lend out $50,000 and could easily get 2 per cent per month on the unpaid balance and frequently even more. I said that I was ashamed to call him my cousin because I have my opinion in relation to this practice and my regard for people who make their livelihood in this manner is very low indeed.
I have already said it is small wonder that the number of Canadians who are

engaging in this kind of enterprise is rapidly increasing. With this in mind I should like to refer hon. members to page 27 of the annual report of the small-loan companies and money lenders. I am using the statistics which appear there simply because I think they are indicative in no small measure of what is happening in the money lending field. We find here the report of the Household Finance Corporation of Canada for the year ending December 31, 1954, in the small-loan field, and I notice that they had a total income of $12,812,433.21. Of that total, Mr. Speaker, they record a profit before income tax of $5,952,743.75. Under their list of expenditure I notice an advertising item of $498,373.17. If you add the advertising expenditures to the profit you get a profit of half of the complete income of this organization. Not only is their profit half of their total income, I notice it is twice the amount of wages they pay. I do not know what their scale of wages is but either it is far too low or the rate of profit is excessive and the interest they are charging is needlessly high.
I also notice there is an investment of share capital paid in cash of $3,070,000. This company in which is invested $3,070,000 was able to pay in dividends to shareholders $3,048,510. In other words, they recovered the whole of their original investment in a 12-month period.
I have available to me a mortgage which was obtained by a mill worker whom I know on a house that would sell for at least $14,000. He needed a bit of money and went to the mortgage company. Apparently he was not able to get a mortgage with reasonable ease so he then went to some of the loan sharks which unfortunately we also have in British Columbia. He signed a first mortgage on his home for $2,300 at 8 per cent and had paid out to him the sum of only $2,000. I have not bothered to work out the interest on that amount.
I have another statistic which I should like to place on the record. The organization to which I am referring is engaged in the business of financing automobile sales. I have a letter from them dated November 10, 1955, which says:
"If the balance is paid by November 30 you will have to send $179.60."
Then on December 12 they wrote:
"The balance is, since no payment was received, $198.47."
A further letter sent at the end of the month again states that the balance is $198.47. In other words, Mr. Speaker, for the loan of $179.60 for one month this company was charging an interest rate of 125 per cent

per annum. If this customer had been foolish enough to have sent the money on December 12 he would have paid an interest rate in excess of 250 per cent. Added to this was compulsory automobile insurance as well as compulsory life insurance. In cases such as this the customer is completely at the mercy of these companies when he applies for a refund.
There may be a reasonable argument raised on behalf of those who have money and decide to lend their money to someone else. After all, if I have a certain sum of money which is legally and rightfully mine I do not have to make that money available for the use of my neighbour, and if I were to do so the argument could be advanced that I should be entitled to stipulate my own terms and conditions and the reward that I would expect for the use of my money.
I think it is fair to say that 90 per cent of the money being used today in Canada for lending purposes does not belong to the lenders. That money is obtained from regular and recognized lending institutions. It is a very common practice when you are engaged in the retail field or in the business of selling automobiles, or even if you wish to set yourself up as a racketeer and open a finance company, that you supply $1 and the life insurance company or the chartered bank will lend you $4 more so that you will have $5 to lend out. Then you pay 4| to 51-per cent interest on that money and as the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) pointed out the other day in the debate on the second reading of Bill No. 10-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Of course the hon. member will not refer to a debate on another bill.

It has been pointed out that this amounts to 400 per cent on the investment. I feel that money in the insurance companies and on deposit with the banks belongs to the masses of the Canadian people and I see something very wrong in people being able to go to those institutions and obtain that money at a low rate of interest and then turn around and lend it back to the people who rightfully own the money at an exorbitant profit.
The argument is sometimes made that the government should not interfere. Let the buyer beware is an old slogan. It is argued that people should acquaint themselves with the rates of interest they have to pay and that these enterprises should be allowed to operate outside the law. These organizations and individuals have the full protection of the law, and when it comes to the customer meeting his part of the contract I submit that if this parliament claims the right to
Interest Act
pass laws which authorize individuals and corporations to collect their pound of flesh then this parliament is morally obligated to pass legislation which will see to it that the customers, the general masses of the people of Canada, get an even break in the deal. We cannot have a law which does not place upon those who use the law for their own protection the duty of being reasonable. Some of the things being done in Canada today are not just or reasonable and legislation is necessary. If we do not want legislation to set maximum interest rates then we should abolish the legislation that enables people to enforce the sanctity of contracts. The one is as fair as the other.
I am also rather concerned with the damage being done to ethical and long-established businesses in our nation. Why should the chartered banks who are engaged in the business of borrowing and lending money not be enabled to extend their activities to meeting the needs of the people? Why should not greater encouragement be given to credit unions? I cannot recall anything important that this government has done to extend the credit union movement, although I realize that on the whole that comes under provincial legislation.
There are many respectable companies engaged in business in Canada, even in the business of lending money. Their reputation and ability to serve the people are being seriously hampered by the activities of these money shysters. Take the retail merchants of Canada, as an instance. I can think of two large furniture establishments operating in Vancouver, both selling on the instalment plan. One store allows for a reasonable profit and if an article is bought on the instalment plan the purchaser pays 9 per cent per annum on the minimum monthly balance. While that may be considered excessive by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) I would tell him that we consider the passage of this bill to be necessary because right in that same city is another large department store which has no markup whatever on its furniture and which openly brags that it sells at cost and makes its money out of the finance fees that are collected. They are putting out of business many of the smaller retailers in the city and they are doing injury to the other large retailer who is attempting to earn a living in an honest way.
I am concerned also with the too liberal credit which is being offered today to the Canadian consumer. I do not think that the easy money available these days is of much help to Canada in the long run. As the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) has pointed out, these high rates are robbing

Interest Act
the Canadian' people of millions of dollars a year. Whatever you charge for the use of money or as an interest rate that exceeds the cost of handling money is the amount of purchasing power that you take from the Canadian people.
I have been told that some members of parliament had very little reaction to the first introduction of this bill a year ago, but that is easily understood. People who are in the clutches of loan companies or instalment buying plans do not go around openly bragging about the fact that they have allowed their finances to get into such a mess. Not many of them would want to inform even their federal member of their situation. We have almost reached the position in Canada where people consider it a disgrace to borrow money. Our forefathers had to borrow money to meet their urgent needs and that was considered a perfectly honourable thing to do and should be so regarded in our society. However, as things are now people hate to admit that they are borrowers of money.
I feel that the government must act this year. I interject again: What about the borrower? I think that this bill will be talked about in Canada for a long time if the government does not act. I am hoping that organizations throughout the country will take up the cause and make enough noise about it that it will reach the ears of the government. I hope that our religious organizations who are concerned with ethics will interest' themselves in the wholesale robbery of the Canadian people which is taking place. I see no reason why those engaged in the practice of lending money or selling goods on time should not be held responsible for the toll that is extracted.
We need money for loans for necessary and worthy purposes. There are many engaged in that occupation in Canada who have a very high reputation. They are concerned with the security of the loan and all they are asking is that the rate allowed be commensurate with the cost of the services they are rendering to society. Finally, I should like to appeal to the government to rid Canadian society of some of these parasites.

I wonder whether the hon. member would permit a question before he finishes. He said he could not remember anything that the house or the government had done to assist the credit unions. I am sure the hon. member will recall that last spring when the bill respecting loans to fishermen came before the house the credit unions were made eligible to make loans in record time, and the bill went through the
[Mr. Regier.l
house much faster than this particular measure is going through the house this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, in answer to the hon. member's question, I believe I did not say that the government had not done anything. Relatively speaking, I felt that way and I believe I started by saying something to that effect but I amended my statement and said that they had done very little. I had in mind the very amendment that the hon. member has mentioned. However, in relation to what the government does to aid private business it has done nothing to aid the credit union movement.
May I ask the hon. member a question? Is he not familiar with the fact that credit unions are granted exemption from taxation under the Income Tax Act?
That is not true. They pay every tax that every other corporation pays.

Mr. Speaker, I would love to answer the hon. member-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Fort William.

Mr. Speaker, there are two sides to this question. I have had some experience with people who borrow and my advice to them has been: Do not buy anything unless you can pay cash. I think that is one thing we should emphasize.
That is easy enough for a $10,000 a year man to say.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Could not the hon. member quote Scripture a little more accurately?

Mr. Speaker, I am going to accept the valuable advice of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) and avoid any quotations from the good book, as he has just suggested. I am very happy to have the opportunity to speak for a few minutes in support of the bill to amend the interest rate which has been introduced by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). I feel he has rendered a service to the house and to the people of Canada by bringing this matter forward. As far as I am able to determine, the time is long overdue for a thorough review of the situation to be undertaken by the House of Commons.
As I understand it, the Interest Act is an act that covers in general terms the whole field of the charging of interest upon money that is lent in Canada. The hon. member proposes to amend section 2 of the act by providing for a maximum rate of interest of 12 per cent. That section now reads:
Except as otherwise provided by this or by the other act of the Parliament of Canada, any person may stipulate for, allow and exact, on any contract or agreement whatsoever, any rate of interest or discount that is agreed upon.
I believe that provision has been on the statute books for a considerable period of time without any change. I do not know exactly when the Interest Act was first placed on the statute books of Canada, but I understand that no amendment to the act
Interest Act
has been made since the year 1907. On various occasions the parliament of Canada has recognized that it is necessary to place curbs upon the unlimited nature of the provisions of section 2 of the Interest Act and has passed certain special acts which limit particular situations as far as the charging of interest is concerned. We have the Small Loans Act, the Money-Lenders Act and the Pawnbrokers Act.
I think that hon. members should be cognizant of the fact that our predecessors have recognized from time to time the necessity of placing restrictions upon the freedom of individuals to lend money at any rate of interest they may be able to obtain. I also think it should be clear from the review of the current situation made by the hon. member for Assiniboia that since the time when such acts as the Money-Lenders Act and the Pawnbrokers Act were placed upon our statute books there have been some very great and drastic changes in the methods of lending money to Canadian citizens. Because of the fact that over a period of time there have come into existence various new institutions or various new methods for lending, such as the credit systems operated by some of our retail chains today, I think the time has now come when it would be advisable to include within this general act an over-all limitation upon any form of money lending which may be undertaken in Canada either as between individuals or through various incorporated money lending agencies so that, as the years go by, those who are concerned in this business will have no loophole through which to devise various other methods within the law of lending money at excessive rates of interest. That is why I feel that the amendment to this act which is being proposed by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) is so greatly to the point.
Some of the hon. members who have spoken have pointed out that over a large field of successful lending operations in this country today interest rates either at 12 per cent or less are enabling money lending businesses to operate with great success, to say the least. While at the time when this act was put on the statute books it might have been a valid argument that if restrictive clauses were attached to this section the field of credit would be unduly limited to those who might have real need of it, nevertheless I think it is fair to say that such is not the situation that exists today. As the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) pointed out, we are today completely surrounded by various agencies that are only too

Interest Act
anxious to make deals that involve the lending of money at interest. As a further instance of that fact, I think it would be worth while at this stage to point out that since the present provisions of this act were established there have arisen in Canada many other fields of lending activity including the whole activity of the credit union movement across this country. That is a movement which has operated successfully within the restriction of the maximum interest rate of 12 per cent. That is a movement which is now sufficiently national in scope to enable all Canadian citizens in need of credit-even if some of these other lending agencies were not in operation-the opportunity to secure credit when they need it.
Apparently the national statistics on credit unions compiled centrally are not particularly up to date; but even in the year 1953 the credit union movement in Canada is reported to have had total assets of $492,384,000 and to have made loans in that year totalling $204,863,000. That fact in itself-to me at least-is an indication of the scope of the present day credit union movement and of the facilities which it has available for making loans to the citizens of Canada. Since their inception and up until the end of 1953, the credit unions across Canada had made loans in a total amount of $1,179,733,000, and they have been growing since 1953. Last year in the evidence given before the banking and commerce committee on the bill to which the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) was referring a few minutes ago, it was indicated that between the years 1954 and 1952 the credit union assets in British Columbia had increased by more than 50 per cent. As I say, while apparently the latest statistics available on a national basis are for 1953, I think it is safe to say that in other parts of Canada the credit union movement has been growing at a comparable rate and that the figures I have just been quoting, if given for the year ending December 31, 1955, would show a material increase over those of 1953.
I have gone to some pains and have spoken at some little length to point out the picture of the credit unions with respect to the offering of credit facilities in Canada. I have done so merely to indicate that, as far as I can see, it certainly would not be valid to argue that any Canadian citizen would be denied an adequate measure of needed credit if the amendment to section 2 of the Interest Act that is proposed by the hon. member for Assinibbia is passed by this house.
As to the situation of the credit unions, I feel that I should mention the fact that in many parts of Canada today the credit unions

are in effect operating as institutions which employ staff on a full time basis and that they have what one might consider to be the normal operating expenses of other lending institutions. Those of us who have had some experience in seeing credit unions start as small organizations know that a good deal of volunteer work has been carried on by the members themselves, and is still being carried on within those organizations, particularly in the smaller places. But in Canada today there are a great many credit unions which have reached the stage where their operations are of such a size that it has become necessary for them to employ a trained staff to carry on their business just as do many of the private commercial organizations. Some of these were mentioned in connection with our fishermen's credit union in the evidence before the banking and commerce committee last year. The largest of those fishermen's credit unions in British Columbia-I refer to the Prince Rupert fisermen's credit union-at that time had assets of $1,750,000 and was making loans on a scale which certainly could not be handled on a volunteer basis. I mention that matter in case somebody might try to suggest that it is not fair to put forward the fact that credit unions can operate quite successfully within a maximum rate of 12 per cent because of the fact that they are carried on by voluntary work on the part of the members.
Without attempting to repeat the arguments that have been advanced by some of the other hon. members who have spoken, and having simply attempted to emphasize one or two of the points which have not been expanded by them, I feel that I can in all conscience urge upon the house the acceptance of the amendment that has been proposed to the Interest Act by the present bill.

There are just one or two comments I should like to make on this bill. I feel that as a parliament we have a duty and a responsibility to our people. The very high cost of living in this country is the concern of all thoughtful Canadians. I suggest that by the passage of this bill we would be making at least a slight contribution towards a reduction in the cost of living. We would be, in effect, increasing to at least a slight degree the purchasing power of the low income groups in Canada.
There are many factors contributing to the high cost of living today. There are such things as the excessive corporation profits, taxation at all levels of government, the effect of the tariff structure on the cost of goods purchased, and of course the excessive debt

charges carried by the people of Canada have a very important part in the high cost of living. Now, anything we can do to lighten the load, we should do. A few moments ago the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) suggested that the parliamentary assistant ought to be thinking about doing something towards reducing the interest rate. But just thinking about it or turning to the government and asking them to take something under consideration is not good enough. Here, we have a specific piece of legislation which will have the effect of benefitting the low income groups in Canada. If the government is at all concerned about helping the low income group, they will support the bill now before the house.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: You have not read the speech from the throne.

We were hoping the parliamentary assistant would take part in this debate and give us some indication of what the government had in mind. However, from past experience with government legislation we know that there is always a great fanfare about legislation that is coming. Then, when the legislation is introduced, we find that in very few instances does it measure up to what it was cracked up to be. For example, at the time the National Housing Act was introduced, we heard a lot of glowing things about the legislation the government was proposing. Since that time we have had ample evidence that the act has not fulfilled the purpose for which it was introduced. We are now told the government is going to introduce some legislation dealing with interest rates. Therefore, we should keep this issue in mind and face up to the fact this bill has the effect of getting to the root of the problem.
This bill is quite clear-cut. It is quite specific. There is no shilly-shallying around, no ifs or buts. It is quite definite, and that is what we regard as the hallmark of a good piece of legislation.
Now, whatever the legislation the government proposes might be, I think that we in this group are going to make it abundantly clear we want some legislation with teeth in it. We want some legislation which is going to do the job we feel must be done at the present time. I repeat that I consider this bill to be at least one step we could take now to ease the burden of our hard-pressed low income groups in Canada. The hon. member for Fort William stated that in his opinion people should not buy goods unless they could pay cash. I wonder how long business would operate in Canada if all businesses adopted the same point of view. Borrowing is an essential part of our whole business structure. It is very easy for
Interest Act
a person with a sizeable income to talk about paying cash, but let us face the fact that if we expect the average Canadian to enjoy some of the amenities of life, if we feel the average housewife ought to have an electric washing machine and some of these other necessary household appliances, then the only way a great many families can buy those things is through borrowing. No amount of lecturing on the part of government supporters is going to change that fact.
Naturally, everyone would prefer to buy for cash. It is the cheapest way to buy. We have all had the experience of going into a store to buy an article priced at say $189. When we announce that we are prepared to pay cash, we usually get a better price. It is, therefore, to everyone's advantage to pay cash. It is all very well for a person with a good income to lecture the poor on the virtues of paying cash, but it is a different matter for a family that is paying exorbitant rents and trying to get the necessities of life to go into the market and pay cash. Unless the government takes it for granted that these people should not have washing machines and these appliances which we have come to regard as household necessities, then I think we ought to be prepared to do something to lighten the load of those who are forced to borrow money to buy these goods.
I believe that from the standpoint of pure economics it is quite obvious that if a person must buy on time or borrow money in order to purchase goods, his purchasing power is reduced considerably. When you multiply the instalment purchases on the part of a great many Canadians from one end of Canada to the other, then you begin to realize the extent to which the purchasing power of the people of Canada is reduced by excessive interest rates. Of course, the effect on business and industry is quite obvious. The less money the individual has to spend on the purchase of consumer goods, the less goods will be purchased. I am suggesting that the passage of this bill bringing about a reduction of interest rates generally will place in the hands of the people more purchasing power, and obviously this additional purchasing power will be used. After all, a family on a low income must spend every penny of that income in order to make ends meet. This money will be spent on consumer goods, and the additional purchases of consumer goods would materially assist the employment picture in this Canada of ours.
When we view this legislation, we must look at it from a broad point of view. Here is a specific example of how we might do something concrete to help the average man,

Interest Act
There are many other ways in which we could help. I mentioned some of the factors contributing to the high cost of living, the tariff structure, the question of corporation profits, taxes and so forth. We must advance in all fields. Looking at this bill now before the house, I suggest it affords every member in this house a definite opportunity of doing something for the people who need help most.
In discussing a bill similar to this the other day which dealt with a reduction in interest rates from 24 per cent to 12 per cent, I referred to the extent to which the people of this country are presently in debt. I placed on the record some figures indicating that there was very little risk involved by the loan companies in lending money. Certainly there is no excuse whatever today for this government permitting loan companies to charge the excessive rates presently being charged because the risk does not warrant them. Certainly, no one is going to suggest that Household Finance, for example, is doing people a favour by lending them money, when they spend nearly $500,000 a year in trying to persuade people to come in and borrow money. One cannot turn on the radio today without hearing some voice saying: "You are welcome at Niagara", or "Come in and borrow money from the friendly finance company". They are spending huge sums of money in order to persuade people to borrow money. They are not doing that as a public service; they are doing that because they know that the lending of money in Canada is one of the most profitable businesses in the country. Apparently the government is prepared to allow them to go on gouging the people of Canada through excessive interest charges.
I am quite willing to admit that many people are not cognizant of the tremendous interest rates they are paying. I believe the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), in a previous debate, referred to the fact that the Canadian Bank of Commerce small loans department found it difficult to compete in some instances with some of the finance companies simply because a great many people were not aware of the disparity in the interest rates because the Canadian Bank of Commerce did not go out into the advertising field and spend a small fortune and charge it, of course, to the fellow who borrows the money. The advertising of the interest rates that he pays is deducted from the income tax of the lending company. Remember, every finance company that is advertising and trying to get people to go into debt is being subsidized by this government in the form of income tax deductions.

No one can rightly say that a great service is being done and that any reduction in the interest rates will drive those people out of the field, or will make credit more difficult to obtain. Remember this, the majority of families in Canada are not in a position to go out and buy a great many of the consumer goods needed in the modern home. The only way in which they can buy those goods is by borrowing money or buying on the instalment plan. You cannot tell me that any level-headed businessman can consider the disappearance of those loan sharks in terms of loss of business. In other words, if he cannot sell his goods he has to go out of business. The lowering of the interest rate certainly is not going to have any effect on the sale of goods through instalment buying, because goods have to be sold and the only way in which they can be sold is by selling them on time.
As I look at this problem from the broad economic point of view, I say we must consider this bill in the light of the effect it will have on the lot of the average family in Canada today. I would venture to suggest that the average low-income family today is in debt, either to a finance company, a department store or a mail order house, and the interest rates which they are paying have the effect of cutting down their purchasing power and thus reducing their standard of living. Therefore, if we are anxious at ail to help the low wage-earning groups in this country, then I suggest a positive way in showing our concern is to pass the bill in its present form.
I suggest that the parliamentary assistant should inform the house now as to the nature of the legislation to be brought down. Is he suggesting that it is the same as this bill? What would be the point of staying out of the debate and suggesting this debate is unnecessary unless the government proposes to bring in almost identical legislation? The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) laughs at that. Mr. Speaker, the arguments which have been set forth by the previous speakers, particularly those from the C.C.F. group, have struck a responsive cord in my being. I agree with them completely that there is a most serious need for some facility whereby the ordinary individual who meets with misfortune can secure himself against a debt which could utterly ruin him throughout the remainder of his life.
Suppose a person, just an ordinary man, working, we will say, for $2,000 a year, has a mishap, for instance the occurrence of a serious case of cancer in his home. He does everything that he possibly can to give his wife, we will say, a chance to recover from the disease. He takes her wherever it seems advisable to take her; he probably takes her to the Mayo clinic and in so doing destroys his financial stability for the remainder of his life, if his wage-earning capacity does not in some way increase. Now, surely any ordinary person realizes it should not be necessary for a man who is placed in circumstances such as these to become the victim of loan sharks .
Take the case of death. No one can possibly escape the consequences of a death in the family. By the time one recovers from the expenses of a funeral, usually they run into the neighbourhood of $500. Let a person borrow $500 at an interest rate amounting to 24 per cent a year; let him be supporting a family which requires all the money he is able to earn, and then let us contemplate the dismal prospects which he faces in life. Then think about that case in terms of the development of communism in the world.
A great many of us are altogether too much inclined to forget that we have been more or less fortunate in life, and it is fortunate. The very best off of us are well-off because of good fortune. The very best that any man can do can fail to win competence in the economic and financial world, without what we call the breaks. What facility have we anywhere in our whole financial and economic structure for providing a person, stricken with a mischance, the like of that which I have indicated, with the means whereby he can go through this experience 67509-514
and emerge with some possible hope of recouping himself, getting on his feet?
I am not prepared to say, Mr. Speaker, that the way of providing for most of the mishaps which I have indicated is through the small-loan company. I sympathize with the points set forth by my hon. friends, but I am not sure that the small-loan companies would be the agencies through which we should endeavour, as an enlightened people in Canada, to provide against the hardships I have indicated and many others which hon. members can think of immediately. I am wondering whether or not we should pass some legislation similar to the Farm Improvement Loans Act or some other of the various acts which we now have such as the Industrial Development Bank Act? I wonder if we could devise some means whereby an agency more or less analogous to those which I have mentioned could be set up from which people who fall upon evil days financially could obtain loans which would enable them to recover economically and financially.
It has been suggested to me by some people that in setting out to solve this problem we could have arrangements with the chartered banks under which the federal government would finance, support or guarantee them in making loans up to a certain amount and under certain conditions, in order that people who are stricken by misfortune would be able to obtain sufficient money to tide them over the period of emergency. It was suggested that an interest rate not exceeding 5 per cent be charged on such loans. I simply throw out that suggestion for your consideration. I have not had sufficient time adequately to think this suggestion through. However, I believe that every hon. member will agree with me that there has long been a need in this country for a facility of this kind. The need is urgent; it is right upon us at the present time.
I well remember when my father died leaving a widow and a family of 13 children on a farm with a 20 year old boy as the oldest breadwinner. The cost of my father's funeral almost sank the family financially. I do not know what would have happened had my father not left a certain amount of assets which could be liquidated. By the time the funeral expenses were taken care of and the succession duties were paid we were very nearly reduced to scratching on gravel. No family should have to face financial difficulties of that kind. No member of any family should have to make the kind of sacrifice which was made by one of the members of my father's family in order that the family could economically survive. I just leave this matter with the house and with the government. I urge that those who have charge

of the financial affairs of our country do not disregard this need. Please do not shrug it off. I urge you to take cognizance of it and to put your best efforts into finding a solution which will actually provide relief for hundreds of thousands of Canadians.

My reason for rising to support the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) is to stress the fact that he has presented to parliament proposals which should receive the sympathetic consideration of hon. members in all sections of the house. I have before me the latest statistical summary issued by the Bank of Canada which points up some facts in connection with charge accounts, retail dealers instalment credit, finance companies instalment credit and cash personal loans from chartered banks.
I suggest that an analysis of what has happened in Canada during the so-called boom would result in some pretty careful consideration. For example, I find that from December 1951, which is apparently as far back as our records go, charge accounts increased from $420 million to $533 million for September 1955, the last period for which statistics have been compiled. In the case of retail dealers instalment credit the increase was from $126 million in December 1951 to $309 million for last September. The finance companies instalment credit increased from $180 million in December 1951 to $575 million, while the cash personal loans increased from $338 million to $790 million. If you add those together you find there has been an increase from $1,120 million to $2,212 million, an increase of over $1,000 million.
Interest Act
I am sure the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance will agree that this indicates a disturbing trend in a country allegedly as prosperous as is Canada. When these statistics reached me I phoned the Bank of Canada to find if it would be possible to get information as to how those figures compared with consumer credit figures for the period prior to the crash of 1928-29, but I was informed that we were not compiling those statistics in Canada at that time. Therefore we have to rely upon statistics supplied by the United States for that period.
It would appear as though this alarming increase in Canada resembles in many respects the increase in credit buying that prevailed in the United States prior to the crash back in 1928-29. It is not hard to figure why there should be this large increase. I am told that nearly anyone who has a clean shirt can go into almost any used car lot in Canada and drive away a car which will run for some considerable time. I am told also that those who are selling radios, television sets and electric refrigerators do not seem to worry very much about the fact that many of their customers are committed to paying more each month than their salaries will permit. That does not seem to disturb many people who are finding that they have to pay interest rates as high as 50 per cent, as was mentioned a few days ago by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Ellis).
It is obvious that the person who cannot pay cash, as was suggested by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), is not going to get out of trouble by paying 50 per cent per annum as interest on the purchase of things which the storekeeper is prepared to sell him. It is bound to get him into trouble eventually.
The latest publication by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) dealing with the distribution of non-farm income in Canada should be examined along with the statistical summary of the Bank of Canada. This publication indicates the staggering information that 34 per cent of Canadian families of two or more persons have an income of less than $2,500 a year; over one-third of Canadian families receive less than $2,500, an average of $1,530.
I think it is pretty obvious that if one-third of our families are getting an average income of only $1,530 annually and cars, radios, electric refrigerators and other electrical appliances are so plentiful on the market and are being pushed, if interest rates of as high as 50 per cent are being charged, there is going to be trouble for someone some time.
If you divide the Canadian families in another way and take those getting less than

Interest Act
$2,000 a year you find that there are 23 per cent or almost one-quarter of the families in Canada of two or more persons who are getting less than that figure per year. If you average the incomes of those 23 per cent you find that it comes to $1,190 per year or less than $100 per month.
You are not going to solve the problem of people in this group if you encourage them to buy television sets, radios, electric refrigerators and what have you by extending credit at interest rates of as high as 50 per cent. Therefore I say that the proposal brought forward by the hon. member for Assiniboia should receive the favourable consideration of hon. members in all sections of the house. We should have legislation which will place a ceiling on these interest rates and assist our friends in the lower income brackets who have such a small average income but who, according to the Bank of Canada, have extended their credit commitments by over $1,000 million since we first started compiling these statistics back in 1951.

I am not able to say as to that, Mr. Speaker. I believe it has just received consideration by the cabinet today in final draft form. That would be a matter on which the cabinet would make the decision, and I would think that decision would be made almost immediately.

I pointed out at that time that he was simply amending one section of the Small Loans Act, and that the effect of his measure neglected the licensing and regulation of small loans in a very wide area. The effect would be that the regulating and licensing provisions elsewhere provided for in the act would simply apply then to only such loans as were made at interest rates between [DOT] 95

of one per cent and one per cent, which as hon. members can recognize is a very narrow range.
So far as the bill we are discussing today is concerned, I do not want to delay the house because I know there are other items under public bills and orders of quite a worthy nature in which private members are interested, and doubtless they want to proceed with them. As I say, there will be another opportunity to discuss this matter. I think some hon. members-including, I believe, the sponsor of the bill-referred to the desire that there should be no charges-I believe that was the word he used-in connection with loans that would involve costs exceeding 12 per cent. I point out to him that in its present form the amendment he has introduced would not ensure that a lender would not be able to make an agreement with a borrower under which the borrower would be obliged to pay, shall we say the insurance premium cost, the cost of drawing up a chattel mortgage, legal fees and various things of that kind which, if taken into account, would be a rather expensive item so far as the borrowing of that money was concerned.
In the Small Loans Act there is a section stipulating that the charges to the borrower must be all-inclusive of not only interest but any other incidental charge related to the borrowing of the money. The hon. member would not accomplish purposes of the kind described in debate by the bill he has introduced today. Therefore when hon. members see the government legislation that is to be introduced almost immediately I think they will realize that the opportunity for a wide discussion of the Small Loans Act will be most beneficial to members of the house before they make up their minds on the question of lending and interest rates generally, particularly when they can see how easy it is to pass legislation such as this that does not take care of costs of all kinds relating to a loan.

The purpose of Bill No. 9 is to amend section 133 of the Income Tax Act. The proposed amendment is not new to this house. Indeed, I have presented a bill in similar terms on several occasions in recent years. Section 133 of the Income Tax Act provides for ironclad secrecy with respect to information obtained through income tax returns. It is our contention that although such secrecy is proper with respect to the income tax returns of individuals, the iron curtain should be lifted so far as corporation income tax returns are concerned.
It is not my purpose, Mr. Speaker, to speak at any length to this bill, for the reason that all the arguments have been advanced a number of times across the years. We feel that corporations are matters of public concern. The business they do affects the economy of the nation. The income taxes they pay either increase the income of the federal treasury, thereby reducing the amount that others have to pay, or their income taxes are reduced, leaving a deficit to be made up by others, notably by individual income taxpayers. Therefore we feel that corporation income tax matters are of public concern, and that it should not be possible for everything in relation to corporation income tax to be carried on behind a wall of secrecy.
I do not suggest in this bill that every corporation income tax return should be printed and made public. Apart from other reasons for not advocating such a proposal, it would involve a tremendous amount of printing that certainly would not be useful or necessary. But we do feel that, particularly where members of parliament believe that information contained in certain corporation income tax returns should be made available, it should be possible for a minister of the crown to give that information. Hence, all this bill does is add to the secrecy provision which is now set out in section 133 this proviso:
Provided that nothing in this section shall operate to prevent a minister of the crown from communicating to the Senate or to the House of Commons any information with respect to corporations obtained under the provisions of this act.
I emphasize again the fact that the proviso which my bill would add to section 133 does not alter the secrecy that now obtains with respect to individual income tax returns.
There are those who have offered as an argument against my bill the suggestion that most corporation income matters are already made public through the annual reports and financial statements which are published by all corporations. I recognize that fact, Mr. Speaker. That is one of the reasons why I do not think we should go to the extent of requiring all of this material to be published
TMr. Benidickson.]

again. But what is not made public, either in the annual financial statements of the corporations or in any other way, is what goes on in arrangements that take place between corporations and the income tax branch.
All of us know, Mr. Speaker, that an individual income tax return, particularly in the case of a great number of Canadian individuals, is a relatively simple matter. The average taxpayer may not call it a simple matter the night he is making out his income tax form, but it is relatively simple. He discovers, for example, that there are not very many deductions he can make. The average taxpayer is limited, so far as deductions are concerned, to contributions he may make to an approved pension plan and to his trade union dues, together with charitable donations and medical expenses. Both those latter items are limited, as set out in the act. I shall not go into the details now.
Beyond those deductions, of course, there are the statutory deductions of $1,000 for a single person and $2,000 for a married person, and a deduction for each child. There are no other deductions that the ordinary taxpayer, filling out the simple form, is permitted to make. As a result there is not much leeway; there is not much question as to what the average individual's amount of income tax will be. It is a very simple matter to work out. But when you come to corporations, the list of items that can be regarded as deductible is very long. In addition, there are the questions of depreciation and all the other kinds of allowances that are provided so far as corporations are concerned.
Obviously, in the very nature of things, when you have so many different factors in the picture as you have with respect to the computing of corporation income tax, there can be a good deal of leeway, a good deal of dispute as to what amounts should be allowed. We all know that these things make a great deal of work for accountants and lawyers, both on the side of the corporations and on the side of the income tax branch.
We have no way of knowing, Mr. Speaker, to what extent certain kinds of expenses are allowed. There is this whole question of advertising. To what extent does one firm get the advertising it claims allowed as deductible before it pays income tax, as compared with the extent accorded to another firm? When is advertising really advertising? When is it political propaganda, or propaganda on the part of an employer against a trade union with which it has a dispute? These are the kinds of things that are involved in arriving at the amount of income tax to be paid by a corporation.
We feel that one corporation as against another should have the right to know what 67509-52

yardstick is being applied, what rules are being used, so there might be fairness as amongst various corporations and so they might know that there is fairness. In addition, we feel the public has a right to know to what extent all of us are really paying for some of the things for which corporations take the credit.
For example, to what extent are we, out of the public treasury, paying for all the advertising with which we are being flooded at the present time? I will not break the rule and refer to the debate that took place earlier today, but I can remind hon. members again that finance companies and loan companies, as well as many other companies, are flooding us, through the press and by radio and television, with a tremendous amount of advertising. We are conscious of the fact that the consumers pay for that advertising in the price of the product, but it is also true that a portion of that advertising is paid for out of the public treasury to the extent that such advertising is allowed as a deductible expense to those corporations. I think that is a matter of public interest and of public concern. I think we should be able to get information as to how much this company or the other was allowed as a deduction for its advertising expenses. That is a type of question that we could get answered if it was not for the ironclad secrecy which is provided in section 133 as it now stands.
I have referred in passing to disputes that take place from time to time between employers and employees. Frequently in such disputes the management will indulge in full page newspaper advertisements stating its side of the case as against that of the union; but when I have asked in the House of Commons as to whether the cost of that advertising was allowed as a deductible expense-in other words, was it being paid for out of the public treasury-I was told that this information could not be given because of the secrecy provision.
So one might go down the list. There are these full page advertisements which the chartered banks publish in the newspapers at the end of the year. I think it would have to be admitted that frequently they are largely political documents. They express views on matters of political concern. Sometimes we in this movement are favoured by being the object of that advertising; sometimes it is pro-government as against the official opposition. To the extent that this sort of thing is political in nature, is it not a fair question to ask if it is being paid for at least in part out of the public treasury by means of an allowance against taxable income before taxes are paid?

Mr. Speaker, I shall be quite brief in contributing to this debate. We are all fairly familiar with the arguments which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has put forward, because this is not the first time he has spoken on this matter.
Parliament has thought it wise to make these returns confidential. The hon. member who has just spoken approves of that in so far as individuals are concerned, but not in so far as corporations are concerned. That seems to me to be unsound. In fact I think you could almost make an argument that in the case of individuals it is only their personal feelings that are concerned but in the case of corporations, if you force them to disclose all the details of their business you may actually injure them in competition. In speaking of competition I think one should bear in

mind that corporations compete not only with each other but with non-incorporated businesses.
Today a friend of mine gave me a rather astonishing illustration of this. He spoke of a case where a certain corporation for which he had worked showed a profit of $2,500, while a certain unincorporated body for which he worked had a profit of over $1 million. I feel the idea which many people hold that corporations are big and individuals are small leads us too far afield. Consequently I want to back to the basis on which this is proposed to be done.
I was rather struck with the fact that the hon. member said the minister should apparently exercise this discretion, and a difficult discretion it would be, at the instance of a Member of Parliament. Now, I am a Member of Parliament, and I should like to be able to think well of myself and of all of my colleagues. However, he seemed to suggest that if a Member of Parliament wanted to go and obtain information from the minister then that was, as I gathered from him, almost a sanction in itself.
As a matter of fact it seems to me that there is a double, almost a triple, objection to the minister having this discretion. As a matter of fact I think it might be argued that there are two objections almost opposite to each other. At that point the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) interrupted to ask, "What is wrong with that?" You are wrong.
