speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Speak a little more loudly, please.

The question with which we are faced is this. To what extent are the government's actions influenced by such contributions from big business? A great many people in Canada today believe that the federal government is being unduly influenced by big business.
Oh, oh.

I hear some hon. members across the floor laughing. I imagine they do not agree with me. I have before me some figures which were taken in a recent public opinion poll in which people were asked who, in their opinion, influences the federal government most. Of the 84 per cent of those who had an opinion to express, 37 per cent said "big business". I think that must include a large number of the Canadian people.
But be that as it may, the question with which we are faced is this. Under the present provisions of the statute the Minister of National Revenue, when a request is made for information with respect to the income tax of a particular corporation, may reply as he has replied in the past-and quite

properly under the present statute-that he is prohibited by the statute itself from giving that information.
What this amendment would do is this. It would not automatically disclose the details of the returns of all the corporations of Canada, but would simply leave to the members of the house the discretion as to whether that information in any particular case should or should not be disclosed. In other words, it would take way that umbrella provision under which the minister at the present time, without justifying his refusal on the grounds of public interest or for any other reason, may simply state that under the statute he is prohibited from giving the information, and that is the end of that. This amendment is an attempt to place the responsibility as to what information shall be given by the government in the hands of the members of this house, where I think it properly belongs.
As representatives of the public we have a right to know what is going on. We must be in a position to answer to these people upon whom taxes are levied and whose money is being spent out of the public treasury. We must be able to answer questions that are put to us. It is a poor position for a public representative to be in when he is obliged to say to his constituents, the Canadian people, "I am sorry, but I cannot give you this information because it is prohibited by statute". Prohibited by whom? Prohibited by the members of this house, because they are the ones who passed the statute in the first place, and they are the ones who must amend the statute if they are going to change the situation. That is what this amendment seeks to do.
Questions arise from time to time. A while ago I mentioned the disclosures that were made by a former member of this house, in which he stated quite frankly that the party of which he was a member-that is the Liberal party-received substantial contributions from various corporations. Various corporation officials themselves have admitted that they make substantial contributions to the party cause. People have a right to know whether such donations or contributions are deductible as an expense when these corporations file their income tax returns. They want to know whether political advertising, which is an indirect contribution to the party's cause, is deductible as a legitimate expense with respect to their income tax returns. They want to know whether in fact the Department of National Revenue collects all the revenue which is lawfully payable to the treasury by the various corporations.

As representatives of the public the members of this house, in their opinion, have a right to be able to assure the public that this matter is being properly handled, that the laws of this country are being properly carried out, and also that the public treasury is not put in the position of being obliged to subsidize any political party in this country, because that is exactly what happens when a corporation may pay for political advertising, make cash contributions or in any way, directly or indirectly, pay into the coffers of the political party in power and, as a return for so doing, be able to deduct that amount as a legitimate expense in making their income tax returns. As representatives of the public we want to be in the position of being able to check on that kind of activity.
That is the main purpose of this amendment. I want to emphasize again, Mr. Speaker, that far from this amendment giving more discretion to the Minister of National Revenue or to any other minister, it is putting the discretion in the hands of the members of this house, where it belongs.
Within the last few days we have been faced with the situation that the government has been in a position to refuse enough information, or to refuse information often enough, without any statute calling for secrecy but simply on the basis that it is not, in their opinion, in the public interest to disclose such information. For example, even this afternoon the Leader of the Opposition was told that the government could not table a certain export permit having to do with the export of arms, not because it was prohibited by statute but because, in the opinion of the government, it would not be in the public interest. We are not even in a position to find out what is being done by private concerns with respect to arms shipments which affect both domestic and international policy.
Without even having a statutory prohibition, there are enough grounds on which the government finds it possible to refuse information. I see no reason why there should be any extra umbrella of secrecy under which they can continue to refuse information which should be in the hands of this parliament.

He is doing this by introducing one of those shadowy measures which will cut at the roots of our economic system.
When the hon. member asks us to vote for a measure which will have the effect of disclosing in this house the income tax returns made by corporations, he is asking something that will reduce the Income Tax Act to nothing. I shall try to make my point on that. It is against the procedure in our courts of justice to have these documents produced and examined by judges. He is asking us to do one thing for one purpose, and next year he will come and say, "Let us do it again for another purpose." The income tax returns would be open to the public and I think that would be the worst thing that could happen in our country. By their very nature these income tax returns are confidential.
I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would not be pleased to have his tax return published in the newspapers of this country. I am sure he is doing right when he makes his return, and I am sure all the people of Canada make honest returns. Let us examine what May says about it. I am taking the citation from Campion, "Introduction to the Procedure of the House of Commons," at page 195:
The rule as laid down by .May page 433 is "a minister is not at liberty to read or quote from a dispatch or other state paper not before the house, unless he is prepared to lay it upon the table."
If, therefore, a question arose in the house about a return made by a corporation, the minister would be forced to deposit the return

Income Tax Act
on the table, because he could not talk about it or refer to it without doing so. In this way all returns made by corporations could be produced, deposited on the table of this parliament and foe open to public discussion. I should think that would be against public security, in the sense that any corporation is entitled to make a return in the knowledge that it will not be made public.
Let us go further; let us go before the courts of justice. It has been acknowledged by the courts of this country that an income tax return is to be considered a confidential document which should not be disclosed in any trial. This rule has been followed, with one exception, by every court in Canada. What will happen to that rule if we vote for this measure introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre? All the returns made by corporations would be tabled in the house and would become public. It would be impossible, therefore, in any trial to keep those returns as privileged documents. They could be introduced in any trial concerning income tax.
In my opinion this legislation is not aimed at the good of Canada, the good of the corporations or the good of the people. In the end it would mean sabotaging the Income Tax Act. If there is one law which has to be protected by this parliament it is the Income Tax Act. I know some people would like to know what there is behind the corporations in this country. It is easy to find out what is behind the big corporations. Their business is well known to everybody. The large corporations advertise the results of their yearly business by publishing reports in our newspapers. Anyone who wants to know these things can find out by looking at the newspapers, and does not need to ask this parliament to make a disclosure of income tax returns.
I do not wish to take much of the time of this house, because it is so precious. However, when I see legislation that is tending toward a system that will bring no good to anyone, I am glad to fight against it. I am of the opinion that this measure is only aimed at the destruction of a system which has built this country, and which is now making this country one of the greatest in the world.

Mr. Speaker, the legislation presented by the hon. member constitutes an amendment to the present Income Tax Act. One should analyse this amendment very carefully. I cannot help thinking that my hon. friend has not given enough thought to its wording. I am rather inclined to think that if the amendment passed it would turn out that he would

eventually get something he did not want. The bill does not make it mandatory for the minister to give information when it is asked for. If it were mandatory perhaps this group would have looked upon it with a little more favour than it does. It would still give the minister a perfect right to withhold information if he so desired. The only thing that would happen is that the minister could not be fined $200 if he did give the information, but if he did not want to he would not have to.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if we examine this amendment more carefully we shall discover that it could be one of the most dangerous pieces of political legislation to have on our statute books. Let me visualize what could happen. I am not saying it would happen. Suppose, for instance, there is a corporation in the province of Saskatchewan in which members of the government have an interest, or some member of the government has an interest. Suppose we take it into the political realm. Let us suppose that a Liberal from Saskatchewan should get wind of something that was unsavoury in connection with that company and should move on the floor of the house for the production of the income tax papers respecting that company. The minister intimates that he is quite willing to give that information and he does so. I would go so far as to say that if there is something unsavoury about it perhaps it should be revealed. Nevertheless this is the picture. He reveals the information and somebody is destroyed. The government of Saskatchewan could conceivably be destroyed.
Let us take another province which we will suppose is a Liberal province. Some member of the opposition gets wind of something that is unsavoury in connection with a corporation, and he moves for the production of the income tax files of this particular corporation. The minister rises in his place and says that he does not think it is in the best interests to reveal the details of that particular case. Of course the house will not get the information then. Therefore I am saying it could be used-I am not saying it would be, because I will not accuse this government of being capable of doing a thing like that-as one of the most dangerous pieces of political legislation we have. I wish the hon. member would give consideration to that. Of course the legislation does not present itself favourably to me or to many of my colleagues. I have not talked it over with all of them.
We are still living under a competitive system. We are still living under a system where we believe that competition is the life of trade. This piece of legislation might be

ail right if there were a socialist government sitting to your right, Mr. Speaker, under which every man's business and every corporation's business could be revealed, if there was a corporation left that was not government-owned. But we in this group still believe in the private enterprise system; we still believe in the competitive system, much as may be desired in respect to it. We do not believe we can take the abuses out of it in this way. In fact it might give rise to even more serious and worse abuses. There should be other ways of doing the same thing.
It could reasonably work in this way. If a corporation has given some funds to the party in office-we know there are some who contribute to the party in power, and some contribute to my friends and some to us, but we do not seem to get very much; corporations and people do support all political parties- it could work out in this way. A corporation may say, "We will give you a donation, but when we give it to you it is going to become public knowledge. If it becomes public knowledge we might lose business, and therefore you see that you take care of us." It could work in that way.
I do not see how the proposed amendment to the Income Tax Act will do what the hon. member wants done. Once again I say, let us have it one way or the other. Let us not leave it to the discretion of the minister. Either leave the thing the way it is or else make it mandatory. Personally I do not think I would be in favour of making it mandatory. We have to give governments a certain amount of authority. They have to collect taxes, and we have to give them the authority to collect without letting the whole nation know everybody's business. That is my view of it. I feel quite certain that if our friends were sitting on the other side of the house they would take the very same view.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, as far as I am concerned I am afraid I shall have to vote against the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, this is a bill to make available to the House of Commons, through the minister, information supplied by corporate taxpayers. In so far as it has been advanced on the basis that it is right and proper, that the House of Commons should be able to call for all information that is necessary or desirable to enable it to discharge its duties, a principle of that kind would commend itself to all members of the house. Parliament can only function if it is able to inform itself. Parliamentary privilege assures that the House of Commons is able to inform itself. If that were the purpose of the bill we might look at it favourably.
Income Tax Act
The other principle of the bill, as I understand it, is that the house suspects the ministry in the way it administers the income tax laws, and wants to obtain information to demonstrate that its suspicions are well founded. We on this side of the house of course know that the ministry deserves suspicion, and that principle certainly commends itself to everyone on this side, but the proper remedy is to turn out the ministry and get one which is above suspicion, and not to go tinkering with somewhat basic legislation.
Looking at the bill itself and the arguments which have been advanced in its support, we see different reasons for this peculiar little bill which appears to be so virtuous and yet has in it the seeds of so much discrimination and snooping. What is the information in question? The information is that which is supplied by taxpayers, all people who are called upon to pay income tax whether they are individuals or corporations. That is information to which the government would not otherwise have access, which would not be gathered in one place if we did not have income tax laws and taxpayers were not required to divulge their income so the government could ascertain with reasonable accuracy whether or not the taxpayer was paying his full tax.
Let us not forget that this information is forced out of the taxpayer for one purpose, and one purpose alone. It is not there to inform all and sundry, to disclose the business of the corporation or of the individual unrelated to the payment of taxes. It is really private information, and the principle of the act has been to keep it private for the purpose of seeing that the income tax due is paid.
As I listened to the arguments presented by the sponsor of this bill I came to the conclusion that apparently his fear was that improper deductions were being made. In other words his fear was that the income tax officials were allowing corporations to make deductions which they were not entitled to make. He suggested certain advertising expenses as an example. He did not suggest any yardstick by which the propriety of deductions could be measured, but I am sure the officials have a yardstick and when they find a corporation has spent too much in advertising an inquiry is made to see just where the money went and to ascertain whether it is properly deductible from income.
We then came down to what seemed to be the real nub of the matter, and that is whether corporations might be allowed to make political contributions and have them

Income Tax Act
deducted from taxable income. I do not consider that there is any difference in principle among the hon. members of this house with respect to the deduction of political contributions. They are not properly deductible as income tax exemptions. If corporations make political contributions they make them out of their own funds, at their own expense. That information is open to any member of the house. Any hon. member could rise in the question period and ask the minister whether or not the political contributions made by corporations are allowed as tax deductions by those corporations, but I am satisfied that is not the principle followed in the administration of the act.
Disregarding the principle, we are urged to inquire into specific cases to see whether or not the ministry is properly enforcing the law. As I suggested previously, the remedy for lack of confidence in the ministry is one that is well known under the parliamentary system; in fact, it is the basis of parliamentary government. Those who supported the bill did not ask the ministry this question. They did not ask the principles on which deductions are allowed. They want instead to snoop into the affairs of certain corporations.
This brings me to the other objection I have to this bill, and which I think every fair-minded member will have. I refer to the fact that it singles out one type of entity in a most discriminating manner. That is to say, it singles out the taxpaying corporation from amongst the taxpayers who are required to supply information, and it does this on no sound basis of distinction and with no principle behind it. The discrimination is between those taxpayers who are corporations and those who are individuals. It is not for the purpose of collecting taxes; it is for the purpose of finding out what political contributions have been made. It does not reach all those who might be interested in making political contributions. There are entities other than taxpaying individuals and corporations, who would not be touched at all by this legislation.
I need not enumerate too many of them to show that there is a discrimination in that respect if the purpose of the bill is what the sponsors have indicated it to be. In the first place, on no sound basis of distinction-I will just elaborate on this for a moment-it leaves cut a person who is in business, who spends money on advertising and who has just as much right as a corporation to deduct this expense from his taxable income. So there is no real difference in principle, as was suggested by the sponsor of the bill.

In fact, all that long list of 46 expenses, with the possible exception of one or two- and I am not sure there are any real exceptions-apply equally to an individual who is carrying on a commercial business as they do to a corporation, because the same expenses are met by an individual in earning a profit and carrying on a business as are met by a corporation, and the individual is properly entitled to deduct all expenses necessarily paid to earn a taxable income. There is a considerable argument in the fact that the individual as well as the corporation is not only subject to inquiry as to the basis of his expenses but there is the first problem which the tax authorities have to determine and that is, what is his income?
There is a good deal of information which may be required to determine that question. What is income may depend on the difficult distinction between what is commonly called a capital gain and what is properly called income or revenue. This distinction which the proposed bill seeks to establish as between an individual and a corporation is entirely without any foundation in reason; therefore I say it is discriminatory. It leaves out the individuals as taxpayers, but it also leaves out individuals who are not taxpayers, nonprofit corporations which are not taxpayers, other corporations which are not taxable, certain co-operatives and trade unions which have been alleged to make political contributions, crown corporations, municipal corporations and other bodies who have funds in their possession which they are free to spend and which are not subject to scrutiny under the provisions of this bill.
For the purpose for which it was designed this bill is a discriminatory measure which no one should consider as sound legislation in amendment of the Income Tax Act, which has been devised after very careful study not only by the authorities and the best brains of the administration but by those who are taxpayers, their various organizations and the community at large.
No; the shaft is aimed at the secrets of the taxpaying corporation alone, with a view to prying into how they spend their own money. The C.C.F. party, which professes to be free of discrimination and to treat all equally, hereby discloses its most common political phobia, abuse of those who endeavour to make a profit.
Hydrophobia.

Not individuals, because individuals have votes and so information as to their profits is not to be included. It is only corporations, which have no votes.

I suggest that the need in the case of corporations is less than in the case of those who are left out of this bill, because the laws of all the provinces and of the federal government require every corporation of any size engaged in a public operation to deliver to its shareholders 10 days in advance-14 days in the case of the dominion-of its annual meeting full particulars of its earnings and expenses, with a balance sheet properly audited and certified by reputable auditors. That is not required of most of the other entities and persons who would not be touched bj this bill.
The bill itself seems to be unnecessary. I suggest that the present section of the Income Tax Act does not prevent parliament from calling for any of this information by a proper order duly passed with the approval of a majority of this house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Members of the hon. member's party have tried that quite often.

The section reads:
133. Every person who, while employed in the service of Her Majesty, has communicated or allowed to be communicated to a person not legally entitled thereto-any information obtained under this act or has allowed any such person to inspect or have access to any written statement furnished under this act is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding $200.
Those are the key words, "person not legally entitled thereto". The question is whether the present section could be read as meaning that parliament is a person not legally entitled to the information. If parliament is legally entitled to the information, then there would be no offence under this section and there would be nothing to prevent parliament asking for a particular bit of information on those occasions when a majority of the house thought it proper to call for it in the usual way by an order for return or whatever procedure might be adopted.
The definition of person is well known. The Interpretation Act defines a person as follows:
(22) "person", or any word or expression descriptive of a person, includes any body corporate and politic, and the heirs, executors, administrators or other legal representatives of such person, according to the law of that part of Canada to which the context extends.
I do not think anyone will argue that the House of Commons is a body corporate or politic under the law of any part of Canada to which the Income Tax Act extends. Furthermore, this section does not prevent the crown from having the information. It is a well known maxim of construction that statutes do not apply to Her Majesty unless so specified. The crown is not "a person not legally entitled" to the information. I am not
Income Tax Act
sure whether a minister is a person; some of them may be, but whether they are legal persons under this act may be doubtful. When you take into account the Interpretation Act as it stands there does not seem to be any real reason in law why it would be an offence for a member of the administration staff of the Department of National Revenue to produce papers called for by an order of this house.
On that account the bill would seem not to be needed, and it does not appear to advance the privileges of the house with respect to obtaining information that it thinks it should have. Therefore I suggest that this measure can only be described as a discriminatory, snooping bill for low partisan purposes.

As everyone knows from common knowledge, from time immemorial the Englishman's home has been his castle, and all matters pertaining to him and his family are protected by law from trespass or exposure. You cannot enter his house without his permission. You cannot ascertain his private affairs without voluntary disclosure. This right of privacy that every Englishman possesses is as strong in this country and in all the countries of the commonwealth as it is and has been from time immemorial in England, from whence we draw so many of our laws and so much of our tradition. This right of privacy that every Englishman possesses is, as I said, as strong in this country as in any other.
These comments are not comments in law. They are comments on things vital to the nation and the welfare of the people, and are instinctively understood, appreciated and jealously guarded by common consent of every citizen in every nation. The provisions of the Income Tax Act respecting the right of the taxpayer to have his appeal heard in camera, and the provisions respecting secrecy which the bill proposes to amend, have been in the Income Tax Act since it was first enacted away back in 1917.
I think it can be taken that these provisions are a recognition of the inherent right of the citizen to have his business affairs kept as private as possible. This right of privacy is necessarily invaded for the purpose of collecting taxes, but when that purpose has been attained these two present provisions of the act preserve to him that right of privacy in all his affairs. The tax laws of all countries of the commonwealth provide that disclosures of their affairs by taxpayers made to tax authorities are to be held confidential and secret.
The taxpayer is by statute compelled to produce and file with the government and its officials for the purposes of revenue, and for the purposes of revenue only, certain portions of his private affairs, namely his income, the contracts out of which his income is earned, his investments, his relations with other businesses, all of which from time to time play a part in determining what the taxpayer's income may be and have to be produced to the revenue officials. On many occasions in litigation between subject and subject litigants in order to advance their case have subpoenaed officers of the crown for the purpose of compelling them in the witness box to disclose information which came into their possession as officers of the

crown under the compulsion of revenue laws, and to compel them to make disclosures. Where the matter was a civil question between subject and subject the courts have sustained the basic British right of privilege or privacy and secrecy pertaining to a man's affairs, and the inroad into those private affairs is not to be made through the medium of subpoenas.
I am informed that the courts have said that while the right of production as an abstract right is not to be denied the courts, it is equally clear that that abstract right is not to be invoked by order of the court to serve the end of litigants in our courts, which are places of public entry. Having secured the abstract right to the courts, they nevertheless realize the paramount need of the nation as a whole and do not issue orders demanding the production of documents which are received under compulsion of law in the course of carrying out a revenue measure.
In cases of litigation in civil courts between subject and subject our Canadian courts have followed the practice of the British courts of maintaining the right of the court to compel the production of any evidence; but where the Minister of National Revenue or his officers state that it would be injurious to the public interest to produce the documents or to give information, they have consistently held that production should not be made or evidence given. I do not attempt to memorize judgments given by courts. Since the hon. gentleman has succeeded in interrupting me, I am going to repeat this judgment of 1893, because it is extremely important. The quotation is as follows:
They (meaning those who are in the public service and the minister in charge of the department) must know the exigencies of the public service far better than the court and therefore the courts, although not departing from the power to have the question thoroughly investigated, nevertheless recognize, in all except extreme cases, that the word of the officer who is the head of the department ought to prevail on the question whether the production of the document would be injurious to the public service.
The courts have dealt with this subject on the broad basis of public policy. Information which is received by the crown for the purpose of revenue only will not be used directly or indirectly in any other direction or for any other purpose. I might interject here, Mr. Speaker, that there have been deviations from that course. For instance, the supreme court decided in 1954 that notwithstanding the section, employees of the Department of National Revenue could be required to classify and produce returns in criminal cases.
My further remarks will have to be with reference to the hearing of these corporate appeals in camera and the necessity that they be kept private and confidential. Court procedures may well expose the trade secrets and every financial operation of a corporation to the full view of its competitors, a process which would completely eliminate the fruits of good business principles and administration and do irreparable harm to the business.
The Income Tax Act gives the minister the widest power to demand information from any person of his own or another taxpayer's affairs for the sole purpose of assessing taxes. That is the reason it is required. Obviously the minister would not of his own volition bring to the house information obtained under the authority of the act. These amendments necessarily mean that somebody in the house or the Senate must seek that information, and the purpose for which he seeks it may be good or evil. Parliament could be made the instrument of securing private information compelled initially to be given by statute, solely for the purpose of revenue; and the house could not possibly know with complete satisfaction why the information in a particular case or group of cases was desired.
It would be my view that parliament is supreme in all these matters. If parliament indicated that this information must be given, we would comply. However, the question that is being put to the test is this. Should this amendment be the means through which persons in this house can cause the minister

to secure information and bring it to the house in response to any inquiry or motion?
I suggest it is more desirable to deal with these matters directly. If any corporation is to be interrogated, or its private affairs examined, then parliament can do so if it so desires, by the appropriate procedure of which every member of this house is aware. That is, it can do directly what this bill seeks to do indirectly.
There are not many more comments that I wish to make, Mr. Speaker, except to say that in addition to the powers of parliament to which I have just referred, the Auditor General of Canada has free access to and has members of his division practically in our head office and in a good many of the more important offices throughout the country. Chapter 116 of the revised statutes of 1952 gives him certain powers. Section 66 of the Financial Administration Act reads as follows:
66. (1) Notwithstanding any act, the Auditor General is entitled to free access at all convenient times to all files, documents and other records relating to the accounts of every department, and he is also entitled to require and receive from members of the public service such information, reports and explanations as he may deem necessary for the proper performance of his duties.
The Auditor General has full authority to examine into the tax returns of any individual or corporation, and he may seek-and he always gets full co-operation and assistance from the members of the Department of National Revenue.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is a matter of pride that the Department of National Revenue has administered this law loyally and meticulously and has complied with all the secrecy provisions, though of necessity the collection of taxes requires the production in detail of the private business affairs of all taxpayers. Should these amendments pass, any resulting disclosure of private information to this house would be disclosure to the public at large, including competitors. That is something which I submit would be resented; and notwithstanding the legality with which these amendments would clothe that disclosure, such resentment would reflect on the administration which had secured the information for the sole purpose of levying taxes.
I am of the opinion that the adoption of these amendments would be a backward step and accordingly I, on behalf of the government, oppose the bill.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister seems to take some pleasure in the fact that the majority of the house happens to agree with him that the proposal set out in this bill should not be enacted. I am aware of the fact that on this measure there seems to be great unanimity amongst the Liberals, the Progressive Conservatives and the Social Crediters in this house. One often hears it said, particularly by Progressive Conservatives and Social Crediters, that parliament should be given full information, that all the matters with which the government is concerned should be brought to the light of day. This is particularly true if the Canadian National Railways is under discussion, or the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, or any other crown corporation, or the affairs of the government itself. All these things must be brought out to the light of day. The veil of secrecy must be lifted.
We put public money into them. You vote public money for them right here.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: My friend the hon. member for Eglinton says that we vote public money. My point is that the amount of money in the public treasury is, to a large extent, determined by the taxes levied on corporations, and the amount obtained from corporations is in turn affected by the treatment accorded to their income tax returns. I contend that this matter is as much a matter of public interest and public concern as are the affairs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the Canadian National Railways, the Polymer Corporation or the government itself.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
My hon. friends shout in holy horror against that view, but it is just a matter of whose ox is being gored. My hon. friends seem quite willing to make their attacks on crown corporations and public bodies, but they want nothing to strike at this sacred privilege of private corporations to enjoy the protection of secrecy. It is interesting to notice the way in which the members of all parties surrounding us get together on this issue.	!
Income Tax Act
Everybody is out of step but Stanley.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I was quite interested in the forthright statement of the position of those opposed to this bill which was given by my good friend the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Boisvert). He went to town; he pulled out all the stops. He said this is something that is sacred; this is one of the most basic things in our society, this right of private corporations to have their income tax matters secret. This is a matter of public security. This is attacking the good of Canada, to attack the secrecy of income tax matters of private corporations.
We contend, Mr. Speaker, that there is no such thing as a corporation-that no corporation in this country would get anywhere- without the people who do the work and who provide the markets out of which these corporations make their income. We contend that these matters are matters of public concern, and that the corporations have no right to the protection of this ironclad secrecy which is given to them by section 133 of the Income Tax Act. It is guaranteed to them, apparently, so long as there are enough Liberals, Tories and Social Crediters in combination to provide a majority in this house.
The Minister of National Revenue makes a good deal of the fact that these corporations are legally persons. I recognize that that is a legal interpretation of a corporation, but surely there is a difference between the Canadian Pacific Railway and James J. McCann or Roland Michener. Surely their being persons is something different than the personality which is ascribed to these corporations. We contend that these corporations should be made the servants of the people, of the living human beings in this country; that they should not have the right to make huge profits out of the economy of this country and have the matter kept in complete secrecy.
Who says the profits are huge?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The Minister of National Revenue, in that part of his speech which was not in the printed speech of last year, said something he was required to withdraw. But in saying that he suggested that some of us were throwing innuendos, were arguing that the income tax department is to be suspected, that it is not to be thoroughly trusted. If the income tax department is completely above suspicion in all its dealing with individual corporations; if it treats every corporation, whether it is the little corner store or a huge distillery, on the same basis with respect to all its different kinds of expenses; I would think it would be the first to say, "We want

Income Tax Act
this material out in the open so there will be no question about it."
This could be described as a bill in defence of the purity of the income tax branch so far as these matters are concerned. I should say very strongly that if there is any matter the people of Canada have a right to know anything about, it is the income tax arrangements with these huge corporations that are making money that they could not possibly make if it were not for the fact that there are 15 million Canadians in this country to do the work and provide the markets out of which this great wealth is made.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Very gladly.
How many of these people are living on what the corporations are doing in this country?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Most of the people in this country are living by the sweat of their brow. Most of the people in this country are living by their toil on the farms or their toil in industry, out of the wages they receive. They are not living out of corporation profits. Only a few are doing that. My hon. friend's approach-

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Does he realize that the government of Canada, for the people of Canada, has a 45 per cent interest through the corporate tax in all the profits of every corporation in Canada? It is that tax that helps to provide-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is exactly the point.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: It is that tax which helps to provide all the social security and other requirements of the country.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I thank the minister for helping me out with my speech. This is something else that was not in the part of last year's speech which he read. He is making the point that the people of Canada, through the government, have a stake in corporate profits to the extent of 45 per cent of those profits. I believe that is one more reason why we should know whether or not that 45 per cent is levied properly and accurately in all cases, whether it is completely fair across the board. It is all the more reason why we should have the kind of information this measure aims at obtaining.
You see, the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Trainor), the hon. member for

Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Boisvert), the Minister of National Revenue and others who might be named seem to think that corporations, because they have payrolls, because they do a certain amount of developmental work, are beneficent feudal lords. They are quite satisfied this is the way our economy should be run. We should bow down and worship these corporations because they provide jobs.
It is our contention, as I have said several times tonight, that no corporation would be able to exist at all in this country, no corporation would make any profit or get anywhere, if it were not for the part that the people play through their toil or through their role as consumers. What we are trying to emphasize is the social fact of what corporations are, and it is because of that social fact we contend we are entitled to such information as is available in the income tax department.
Tell us about the socialist corporations.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
A number of my friends raised an interesting question. They wanted to know whether I was not being discriminatory in distinguishing between individuals and corporations. I point out, of course, that the Income Tax Act distinguishes between individuals and corporations. There are the two groups. There is the individual income tax and the corporate income tax.
I point out also that when I first introduced this bill, and as the Minister of National Revenue says that was a long time ago, its provisions were not limited to corporations. When I first introduced the bill it called for the possible revelation of this information from any income tax return. There are still 50 or more hon. members around who were here when I first introduced this bill, and if they will search their memories they will realize that the main criticism levelled at my bill when it included individual income tax returns was that this was peeping Tom legislation; this was getting into the private affairs of individuals. All the attacks on that first bill of mine were levelled against the extent to which it seemed to get at individuals. I said all right; if that seems to be the main criticism of this bill I will accept it and take out the part regarding individuals, just leaving the corporations. The fact is that far more holy horror is expressed now when an attempt is made to get information concerning corporations alone than was expressed when it related to individuals. We know now who the sacred cow is so far as the other three parties of this house are concerned.
Go on with your hymn of hate.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
My hon. friends can make these interjections if they wish. They are simply making it clear that their concept of public service is to provide special privilege for monopolistic corporations, even in a day when society has moved on to the realization that most of the things we do are by common, community, co-operative effort; what we gain we gain by our common effort, and what we have won in that way really belongs to us all-at least, the knowledge about it, such as that which is in the possession of the Department of National Revenue.
Some of those who have criticized the bill, notably the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell), have asked questions about the mechanics of it in the form in which it is drafted. The hon. member for Macleod implied that if the publishing of this information by the government were made mandatory by my bill instead of voluntary, his attitude toward it might have been different.
He said he did not think so.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Well, I have a pretty good idea what would have been said by him and by others in this house if I had brought in a bill making it mandatory to publish all the information in all the corporation income tax returns filed with the Department of National Revenue. I would have been told it would involve a huge amount of printing; it would involve an endless and wasteful expenditure, and therefore we simply could not go ahead with it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, despite the charges that have been made that I did not think this thing through too well before I drafted this bill, I make the assertion that I did do a great deal of thinking about it and did discuss it with legal counsel as well, as to what was the best'way to go about it; and it was quite a deliberate decision on my part that one should not require that all the information should be published automatically but rather, as the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) put it, that the umbrella under which the Minister of National Revenue can now hide should be removed, and moreover that the legislation should be such that a minister of the crown could give this information in the Senate or in the House of Commons.
The bill as worded does not require such information to be requested by a member of parliament. Indeed, the minister could make such information public on his own initiative; but I suggest that the hon. member for Macleod is really handing out innuendoes when he suggests that if this bill were passed any minister would take the position in reply to one request that that kind of information could be given, but in reply to another, which
Income Tax Act
might be embarrassing to his side of the house, that information would be withheld.
I did not say that. I said it was conceivable that that could happen.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The hon. member said it was conceivable. I am sure that if he will read the bill more carefully and think it through he will realize that if it were passed, not to be mandatory that everything be published but with a provision for the minister to make any of this information available to parliament, I suggest it would be an affront to parliament if any minister after that refused to give any information of that kind that was requested.
Some have said that parliament can get action today. The hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Michener) said that parliament can pass the appropriate order for return and get the information, but the Minister of National Revenue does not agree with the hon. member for St. Paul's on that point. On February 21, 1955, as recorded at page 1331 of Hansard, my colleague the hon. member for Dauphin moved a motion calling for certain documents in this field. This was the reply of the Minister of National Revenue:

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will have to oppose this motion, and suggest to the hon. member that it be withdrawn. I oppose it on the ground that this is private correspondence between a taxpayer and the taxation division of the Department of National Revenue and that, according to the secrecy provisions, it cannot be disclosed.
I remind the hon. member for St. Paul's that last year when we were dealing with a certain question his colleague, the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), sought to get certain information. He was told, as I was told at the same time, that we could not get that kind of information because of the secrecy provisions of the act.
Because the order was not passed.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: My hon. friend says: "Because the order was not passed". Does he not know that at the present time there is in this house an overpowering majority that defeats motions of that kind every time? And does he not realize that he himself admitted that if by any chance his party were on the other side they would take the same stand? He said that tonight.
No, he did not.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Oh, yes.
He did no such thing.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
He said that the way to correct what he thought might be some doubt-

Income Tax Act
ful practices in the Department of National Revenue was not to lift the veil of secrecy; no, keep it on, just change the party in power.
On a question of privilege, what I suggested was that if the house by a majority called for those papers there was nothing in the act as it stands to prevent them being given.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
That is a debatable point. I do not think the Minister of National Revenue will agree with the hon. member that they could be brought down even if the house passed the motion, since it is against the statute. If I may offer my opinion, even though I am not a lawyer, the only way the house could override a statute would be by passing another statute, not simply by an order for return, as my hon. friend suggests.
But the point is-and the hon. member for St. Paul's has made his party's position clear in this matter-that so long as the majority is against this kind of thing we will not get it. We know the Liberals are against it. We know now the Conservatives are against it. We know the Social Crediters are against it. It looks as though the secrecy surrounding private enterprise is protected, and therefore for some little while longer private enterprise can go its merry way knowing that its affairs, though they are of public concern, though they are possible only because of the contribution the public makes to them, will not be made known to the people of this country.
This is a longer speech, Mr. Speaker, than I made when I introduced the bill. At any rate, nobody would say I am reading it, or that I ever read a speech in this house.
Maybe you cannot read.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I hear someone say, "Maybe you cannot read". That might be correct. I am also aware of the fact that when I introduced the bill I thought, well, it is just a harmless little bill. The rest of the boys, and the girls, do not like it, but it will not stir them up too much. But lo and behold, it has. It has stirred them up as it did before because of the interest so many members in this house seem to have in protecting private enterprise and the profits that huge corporations make out of the Canadian people.
Some day there will be a change. Some day the people of this country will realize that the economy of this country is a matter of public concern, and that all its benefits should accrue to the people of Canada themselves.

The house resumed, from Thursday, January 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Holling worth:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to provide national scholarships and bursaries for students at the university level who are in financial need, in so far as the subject matter of this resolution is within the competence of parliament.

subtopic: PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must congratulate the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) upon presenting this resolution to the house. It is significant that the members of all parties have paid tribute to my colleague the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) for having presented a similar resolution to parliament year after year. Now that hon. members of all parties have indicated their support of the ideas expressed in this resolution I hope that action will be taken very soon and funds made available for this purpose.
When we consider the amount spent by the Canadian people on educating our young people during the war years it is clear that we are going to have to tackle the problem of providing funds for university education just as we provided funds during the war years.
I remember that during the war a question was asked of Senator Power, who was then minister of national defence for air, as to the cost of training a pilot. He said the cost was around $30,000. A year ago the present Minister of National Defence was asked the same question, and he said the cost is now $65,000. If the people of Canada are able to spend $65,000 on the training of a pilot, we can spend adequate amounts to provide university education.
This morning I ran across a new book, "The Age of Mackenzie King". I am sure that all members of parliament will want to read this very interesting book written by H. S. Ferns and B. Ostry. I find that the book is dedicated to the memory of Flying Officer William Paterson and Pilot Officer Leon A. Titof. Those members who were here in 1940 will recall that Flying Officer Paterson was on the prime minister's staff at that time. He was a very brilliant young Canadian who had started out in external affairs and was then in the prime minister's office.
I remember being in the home of our station agent on Christmas eve, 1943, I think it was. The year before the station agent had received word that his only son, who was in the R.C.A.F., had been reported missing. Later the news of his unfortunate death was received. Flying Officer Paterson was overseas with the R.C.A.F. and on Christmas morning his wife received word that he was missing. Later it was confirmed by the R.C.A.F. that he would never come back to Canada. Pilot Officer Titof also came from my constituency. His father was a merchant, and this young chap was able to join the air force when he finished school. He was such a promising young lad, and of course he never came back.
Recently I saw some statistics prepared by the Canadian Bank of Commerce indicating the division of federal, provincial and municipal taxes. The breakdown to the nearest percentage showed that of the Canadian tax dollar, 74 per cent comes to the Minister of National Revenue and 14 per cent to the provincial treasury, with 12 per cent going to the municipality. I think it must be obvious to everybody that the municipalities and the provinces with but 26 cents of every tax dollar provided by the Canadian people cannot furnish that quality of education which is necessary in this day and age.
When one considers that thousands of our young people had similar experiences to those of Flying Officer Paterson and Pilot Officer Titof one might expect that now, in memory of these young men and their pals, we would find ways and means to see that the young people of Canada who have the mental qualifications are given a chance to go to university and make their contribution to the life of Canada and of the world.
Therefore I hope there will be unanimous support for the resolution moved by the hon. member for York Centre. I hope we will all accept the resolution.

Education

subtopic: PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words in support of the resolution of the hon. member for York Centre, which I think is supported in most quarters of the house. Before I do so, however, I should like to make one point that has not been made yet.
While it does seem to me that we need more of the right kind of students in all our educational institutions, the primary schools, the high schools and the universities, I think we now have a great many of the wrong kind of students at all levels of our educational system. It seems to me that not only in the higher grades of our primary schools but in our high schools and in our universities there are people who do not want to be there, who are kept there more or less against their wills, either through family pressure or other pressure, who are only marking time. The net effect of their presence is to clog the progress of all. I think these beliefs would be borne out by almost anyone who acts in a professional capacity at any level of our educational system in Canada. In other words we have too many drones, too many dead cells, in our educational institutions.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, I think t must be obvious to anyone who studies the facts that there are a great many potential leaders in all walks of life who never get the shance to become leaders in our society aecause they lack the opportunity to get such education as would enable them to do so. I ;hink the very first point made yesterday n the joint declaration by the two great eaders of the western democracies, President Eisenhower and Sir Anthony Eden, centred >n the value of the individual.
It seems to me if there is one thing that differentiates our ideals from the ideals of certain other parts of the world it is that we place as the supreme value the worth of the individual citizen in our democracy; and it is a fact that is easily ascertained by studying what happens in any walk of life in our society that a great many people who are potentially great in any field do not get a chance to make the most of their talents simply because they lack the education.
I move the adjournment of the debate.

1.	Was a brief submitted to the Minister of Finance, the Acting Postmaster General and the Secretary of State, on May 27, 1955, by the postal workers' brotherhood of Canada, asking for an increase in their salaries?
2.	If so, has consideration been given by the government to this request and what decision was made?
3.	Has the government given consideration to the setting up of a board of arbitration or commission to hear representations and to make recommendations relative to the request by the said brotherhood?
Answer by: Mr. St. Laurent (Quebec East):
1.	Yes.
2.	Yes; no general increase in civil service salaries has been made since the request. The brotherhood was told that ministers had not been convinced there is a justification for special action in regard to the salaries of postal workers, but they would be glad to see any further evidence that the brotherhood wishes to present in support of its case.
3.	No; the Prime Minister informed the brotherhood that the Civil Service Act did not provide for arbitration and the law relating to conciliation boards in industrial disputes is clear in stating parliament's intention that it should not apply to the civil service. It was pointed out that the civil service commission is an independent body, established by parliament and not subject to any direction by the government, which has the duty of investigating questions of the kind referred to by the brotherhood, hearing the views of associations and making recommendations upon them. The Prime Minister expressed his view that this full-time tribunal, established by parliament and assisted by a large and expert staff, is far better able to give proper consideration to matters of this kind than would some ad hoc conciliation board as proposed by the brotherhood.
